tenancy.intro: Things the landlord may bring that are not in your files yet. We list them so you are not surprised at the first court meeting. Answer each one.
tenancy.note: The landlord can make a claim back against you, up to 3 days before the first court meeting. Your evidence list is your answer to it.

questions.q: Could the landlord have their own photos of the flat or furniture, taken after you left?
questions.hint: Your own dated move-out photos or video are the answer. Keep them.

questions.q: Has the landlord sent, or could he get, a repair or cleaning invoice?
questions.hint: Ask for it in your written request. The court has a form where each fault and its cost is listed.

questions.q: Did you sign an inventory or handover form?
questions.hint: Check your agreement for an inventory clause. Get your copy. If it lists the item, it matters either way.

questions.q: Were there any other agreed conditions, spoken or in messages on any channel? Cleaning, repainting, bills, keys.
questions.hint: Check SMS, email and other apps you used with him. Anything agreed can change what he can hold back.

questions.q: Did anyone else see the handover? A friend, mover or agent.
questions.hint: Write down their name. You can name them as a witness later.

questions.q: Did you accept any deduction, even in passing?
questions.hint: If yes, say how much and when. It changes the amount you claim.

goods.intro: Things the seller may bring that are not in your files yet. We list them so you are not surprised at the first court meeting. Answer each one.
goods.note: The seller can make a claim back against you, up to 3 days before the first court meeting. Your evidence list is your answer to it.

questions.q: Could the seller have a signed delivery note or an inspection record?
questions.hint: Check what you signed on delivery.

questions.q: Did the listing or terms say the goods were sold as seen, used, or without warranty?
questions.hint: Re-read the listing and any terms page.

questions.q: Did you tell the seller about the fault within a reasonable time, in writing?
questions.hint: Find the first message where you raised it and its date.

questions.q: Did anyone else use, repair or open the goods before you complained?
questions.hint: The seller may say the fault came later.

questions.q: Did anyone else see the goods when they arrived or when the fault showed?
questions.hint: Write down their name. You can name them as a witness later.

questions.q: Did you accept a partial refund, repair or replacement, even in passing?
questions.hint: If yes, say what and when. It changes the amount you claim.

general.intro: Things the other side may bring that are not in your files yet. We list them so you are not surprised at the first court meeting. Answer each one.
general.note: The other side can make a claim back against you, up to 3 days before the first court meeting. Your evidence list is your answer to it.

questions.q: Could the other side have their own photos, records or receipts about this?
questions.hint: Think about what they would show a judge. Keep anything of yours that answers it.

questions.q: Did anything you signed or agreed to limit what you can claim?
questions.hint: Re-read the contract, quote or terms for words like as is, no refund, or a cap.

questions.q: Did you tell the other side about the problem in writing, soon after it happened?
questions.hint: Find the first message where you raised it and its date.

questions.q: Were there other agreed conditions, spoken or in messages on any channel?
questions.hint: Check SMS, email and other apps you used with them. Anything agreed can change the claim.

questions.q: Did anyone else see what happened?
questions.hint: Write down their name. You can name them as a witness later.

questions.q: Did you accept any part payment, repair or discount, even in passing?
questions.hint: If yes, say what and when. It changes the amount you claim.
